fact_text: A Venezuelan national is visa-required for Ireland and must obtain a long-stay 'D' employment visa BEFORE travelling to take up employment for more than 90 days. Venezuela appears in none of Ireland's visa-exempt categories: EEA, UK and Swiss citizens; the published table of further visa-exempt nationalities; or holders of an EEA or Swiss residence card issued as the family member of an EEA or Swiss citizen exercising free movement.

non_obvious_note.official_guidance: Nationals of the UK, Switzerland and the EEA do not need a visa for Ireland.
non_obvious_note.actual_reality: Venezuela is a visa-required nationality, so a long-stay 'D' visa must be granted before travel even though the person already lives in the EU (Spain).
non_obvious_note.action_required: Apply for the Irish long-stay 'D' employment visa before booking travel; do not travel on the employment permit alone.

source_name: Citizens Information — Visa requirements for entering Ireland
evidence_quote: If you are travelling to Ireland and you are not a citizen of the UK, Switzerland, or a country in the European Economic Area (the EU plus Norway, Iceland and Lichtenstein), you may need to apply for a visa.

fact_text: The correct entry route for employment lasting more than 3 months is the long-stay 'D' visa (as opposed to a short-stay 'C' visa).
source_name: Citizens Information — Visa requirements for entering Ireland
evidence_quote: If you want to come to Ireland for more than 3 months, for example to study, for work or to settle permanently in Ireland with family members who live in Ireland, then you can apply for a long stay 'D' visa.

fact_text: The 'D' employment visa can only be applied for AFTER the employment permit has been granted, up to 3 months before the travel date; a decision takes approximately 8 weeks. Sequence: permit granted -> visa applied for -> visa granted -> travel.

non_obvious_note.official_guidance: You apply for an employment visa once you hold an employment permit.
non_obvious_note.actual_reality: The permit (DETE) and the visa (ISD) are two separate authorisations from two authorities in sequence; the ~8-week visa wait sits on top of the permit wait and defines the real pre-arrival runway.
non_obvious_note.action_required: Front-load the permit application so the visa can be lodged up to 3 months before the intended start date.

evidence_quote: Once you have received a permit, you are eligible to apply for an Employment Visa.

fact_text: The visa application is made from the applicant's home country or country of legal residence — for a Venezuelan legally resident in Spain, that is the Irish visa facility handling applications from Spain, not Venezuela.
evidence_quote: You must apply from your home country or where you are a legal resident.

fact_text: A Spanish residence card / TIE (including EU long-term resident status held in Spain) does not by itself grant the right to enter or work in Ireland. Ireland is outside the Schengen area and is not bound by the EU Long-Term Residents Directive 2003/109/EC, so residence in another EU state confers no visa-free entry for a visa-required national. There is one exception: a residence card issued by an EEA country or Switzerland to the family member of an EEA or Swiss citizen who is living outside that citizen's own home country does remove the Irish visa requirement.

non_obvious_note.official_guidance: Residence in one EU state does not, by itself, give entry rights to Ireland.
non_obvious_note.actual_reality: Ireland is not in Schengen and is not bound by the EU Long-Term Residents Directive 2003/109/EC; a Venezuelan holding an ordinary Spanish TIE still needs an Irish 'D' visa. This is the single most expensive misconception for movers who have 'already lived in the EU for years'. The exception is narrow but decisive: where the Spanish card was issued because the holder is the family member of an EEA or Swiss citizen exercising free movement in Spain — an EU spouse who is not Spanish — no Irish visa is required.
non_obvious_note.action_required: Establish which basis the Spanish card was issued on. For an ordinary work or long-term-resident TIE, treat the move as a full third-country entry: permit -> Irish 'D' visa -> IRP registration. Where it was issued as the family member of an EEA or Swiss citizen exercising free movement, confirm the exemption before applying for a visa.

source_name: Citizens Information — Visa requirements for entering Ireland
evidence_quote: If you are travelling to Ireland and you are not a citizen of the UK, Switzerland, or a country in the European Economic Area (the EU plus Norway, Iceland and Lichtenstein), you may need to apply for a visa.

fact_text: A Critical Skills Employment Permit allows IMMEDIATE family reunification — the spouse/de-facto partner and dependent children can apply to come to Ireland with no waiting period. (A General Employment Permit imposes a 12-month wait.)

non_obvious_note.official_guidance: Employment permit holders may sponsor family reunification.
non_obvious_note.actual_reality: The Critical Skills permit's immediate reunification, against the General permit's 12-month wait, is decisive for anyone moving with a spouse, partner or dependent children, and should shape which permit is pursued.
non_obvious_note.action_required: Confirm the role qualifies for CSEP (Critical Skills Occupations List) so the family can travel together.

source_name: Citizens Information — Employment permits and family members
evidence_quote: Your spouse or de facto partner and dependent children can apply to come to Ireland without any waiting period.

fact_text: The spouse or partner of a Critical Skills Employment Permit holder is registered on a Stamp 1G on arrival, which gives the right to work in Ireland WITHOUT a separate employment permit.

non_obvious_note.official_guidance: Family members of permit holders may seek employment.
non_obvious_note.actual_reality: Stamp 1G means the accompanying spouse can take any job immediately with no employer sponsorship. Since 15 May 2024 the spouse or de-facto partner of a General Employment Permit or Intra-Corporate Transferee holder can also work without an employment permit, so the advantage distinctive to the Critical Skills route is the immediate family reunification — no 12-month wait — rather than the right to work itself.
non_obvious_note.action_required: Register the spouse for their Stamp 1G IRP after arrival; no employment permit is needed for them to work.

source_name: Citizens Information — Employment permits and family members
evidence_quote: Your spouse or partner can get a Stamp 1G IRP when they register. This gives them the right to work without an employment permit.

fact_text: Visa-required family members (a Venezuelan spouse and children) must be granted an Irish 'D' — Join Family visa BEFORE coming to Ireland. They cannot travel on the permit holder's status alone.

non_obvious_note.official_guidance: Family members join the permit holder in Ireland.
non_obvious_note.actual_reality: Each visa-required dependant needs their own Join Family 'D' visa granted before travel — a separate application track that must be planned alongside the principal's visa.
non_obvious_note.action_required: Lodge a Join Family 'D' visa for each visa-required dependant; align timing with the principal's move.

evidence_quote: If you require a visa to travel to Ireland you must have been granted an Irish 'D' - Join Family visa before coming to Ireland

fact_text: The Critical Skills Employment Permit needs NO Labour Market Needs Test. Minimum annual remuneration: EUR 40,904 for occupations on the Critical Skills Occupations List (with a relevant degree), EUR 36,848 if the applicant qualified within the prior 12 months, or EUR 68,911 for occupations not on the list. After the permit, the holder can apply directly for a Stamp 4.
evidence_quote: Because the skills are identified as being in short supply, a Labour Market Needs Test is not required.
